topics.name: curate
topics.title: curate() Function
topics.summary: This function curates a data.frame of N gates and the sets of events immediately linked to those gates.
topics.description: This function curates a data.frame of N gates and the sets of events immediately linked to those gates.

arguments.name: nodes
arguments.description: (Required) data.frame of N nodes (1 to N rows), with a unique id for each node, an event name describing the node (some events occur multiple times), and a type vector categorizing nodes as "and" | "or" gates, "top" nodes, or "not" a gate or top node (ie. a normal node)

arguments.name: edges
arguments.description: (Required) data.frame of N edges (1 to N rows), showing ties between the from node's id to the to node's id.

topics.value:
A data.frame (tibble) with one row per gate, containing:

  • gate: Character vector of gate/event names
  • type: Factor or character vector indicating gate type ("top", "and", or "or")
  • class: Factor with levels "top" and "gate", classifying nodes as top events or intermediate gates
  • n: Integer count of events immediately connected to this gate
  • set: Character string containing the boolean expression for this gate's inputs, using * for AND operations and + for OR operations, wrapped in parentheses
  • items: List column containing character vectors of event names that are inputs to this gate

Rows are sorted with top events first, followed by gates in alphabetical order.
topics.details:
This function performs the initial curation step in the fault tree analysis workflow:

  • Filters nodes to only gates and top events (excludes basic events with type == "not")
  • Joins edge information to identify which events connect to each gate
  • Converts gate relationships into boolean expressions: AND gates use * (multiplication), OR gates use + (addition)
  • Wraps each gate's set expression in parentheses to preserve order of operations
  • Creates both string (set) and list (items) representations of gate inputs for different downstream uses

The output serves as the foundation for subsequent steps: equate() uses the set column to build the complete boolean equation, while mocus() uses the items list column for cutset generation.
topics.examples:
# Load dependencies
library(dplyr)
library(tidyfault)

# Load example data into our environment
data("fakenodes")
data("fakeedges")

# Build the gate-level representation used by downstream functions
gates <- curate(nodes = fakenodes, edges = fakeedges)
gates

# Example downstream workflow from curate() output
formula <- gates %>%
   equate() %>%
   formulate()
gates %>%
   concentrate(method = "mocus_rcpp") %>%
   tabulate(formula = formula, method = "mocus_rcpp")
topics.seealso: equate() for building the complete boolean equation from curated gates, illustrate() for visualizing the fault tree structure

topics.name: equate
topics.title: equate() Function
topics.summary: This function extracts the equation for a fault tree from a data.frame of gates and sets, outputted by curate().
topics.description: This function extracts the equation for a fault tree from a data.frame of gates and sets, outputted by curate().

arguments.name: data
arguments.description: (Required) data.frame of N gates, containing columns for gate, type, and set. Outputted by curate(). Must have at least one row with class == "top" representing the top event.

topics.value:
A character string containing the complete boolean equation for the entire fault tree. The equation:

  • Uses * (multiplication) to represent AND operations
  • Uses + (addition) to represent OR operations
  • Contains only basic event names (no gate references)
  • Is wrapped in parentheses to preserve order of operations
  • Represents the top event's boolean logic in terms of all basic events

This equation can be passed directly to formulate() to create an executable function.
topics.details:
This function builds the complete boolean equation through an iterative substitution algorithm:

  • Starts with the top event's set expression, which may contain references to other gates
  • Iteratively replaces each gate name with its corresponding set boolean expression
  • Continues until no gate names remain in any expression (only basic events remain)
  • Returns the fully expanded equation from the top event (first row of the data.frame)

The algorithm processes gates in order and handles nested gate structures by repeatedly substituting until convergence. The substitution preserves the boolean operators (* for AND, + for OR) and parentheses structure created by curate().
topics.examples:
# Load dependencies
library(dplyr)
library(tidyfault)

# Load example data into our environment
data("fakenodes")
data("fakeedges")

# Build gate-level representation and expand to a full boolean equation
gates <- curate(nodes = fakenodes, edges = fakeedges)
equation <- equate(gates)
equation

# Example downstream use of equate() output
formula <- formulate(equation)
calculate(formula)
topics.seealso: curate() for creating the gates data.frame, formulate() for converting the equation string into an executable function

topics.name: formulate
topics.title: formulate() Function
topics.summary: This function formulates a character string (the boolean equation of a fault tree) into an R function that evaluates system failure.
topics.description: This function formulates a character string (the boolean equation of a fault tree) into an R function that evaluates system failure. Handles AND and OR operations.

arguments.name: formula
arguments.description: (Required) A character string containing the boolean logic equation of a fault tree. Should use * for AND operations, + for OR operations, and parentheses for grouping. The equation should contain only basic event names (no gate references). Typically output from equate().

topics.value:
A function object that:

  • Accepts named arguments for each basic event in the formula
  • Each argument accepts numeric values (typically 0 or 1 for binary events)
  • Returns a numeric value representing the system state (typically 0 for no failure, >= 1 for failure)
  • Evaluates the boolean equation using R's arithmetic operators (* for AND, + for OR)

The function can be called directly with event values or passed to calculate() to generate a complete truth table.
topics.details:
This function converts a boolean equation string into an executable R function through the following process:

  • Extracts all unique event names from the formula by splitting on operators (+, *, (, ))
  • Creates formal arguments for the function, one for each unique event name
  • Sets the function body to parse and evaluate the formula string
  • Returns a function that can be called with named arguments for each event

The function uses R's arithmetic operators where multiplication (*) represents AND logic and addition (+) represents OR logic. When called with binary inputs (0/1), the function returns 0 for no failure and a positive value for failure. The function preserves the order of operations through parentheses in the original formula.
topics.examples:
# Load dependencies
library(dplyr)
library(tidyfault)

# Load example data into our environment
data("fakenodes")
data("fakeedges")

# Build a boolean equation and convert it to an executable function
equation <- curate(nodes = fakenodes, edges = fakeedges) %>%
   equate()
formula <- formulate(equation)
formula

# Evaluate across all combinations of basic events
calculate(formula)
topics.seealso: equate() for generating the boolean equation string, calculate() for generating truth tables from the function

topics.name: calculate
topics.title: calculate() Function
topics.summary: This function takes a supplied function f and computes the system failure outcomes (1 = failure vs. 0 = not) given every possible combination of input events failing (1) or not failing (0).
topics.description: This function takes a supplied function f and computes the system failure outcomes (1 = failure vs. 0 = not) given every possible combination of input events failing (1) or not failing (0). Outputs a data.frame.

arguments.name: f
arguments.description: (Required) Function outputted by formulate(), including arguments for all input events in the fault tree (excluding gates or top events). The function should accept binary (0/1) arguments for each basic event and return a numeric value.

topics.value:
A data.frame containing a truth table with:

  • One column for each input event (named according to the function's formal arguments)
  • An outcome column indicating system failure (1) or no failure (0)

Rows are arranged in descending order by outcome, with failure cases listed first. The truth table contains 2^n rows where n is the number of input events, representing all possible combinations of event states.
topics.details:
This function generates a complete truth table by:

  • Extracting the formal arguments from the supplied function to identify all input events
  • Creating a grid of all possible binary combinations (0/1) for each event using tidyr::expand_grid()
  • Evaluating the function for each combination to determine system failure
  • Converting outcomes to binary: any value >= 1 indicates failure (1), otherwise no failure (0)

The function is designed to work with boolean functions created by formulate() that represent fault tree logic. The outcome threshold (>= 1) allows for functions that may return counts or probabilities rather than strict boolean values.
topics.examples:
# Load dependencies
library(dplyr)
library(tidyfault)

# Load example data into our environment
data("fakenodes")
data("fakeedges")

# Build fault tree function and generate full truth table
formula <- curate(nodes = fakenodes, edges = fakeedges) %>%
   equate() %>%
   formulate()
truth_table <- calculate(formula)
truth_table

# Optional downstream use with MOCUS minimization
curate(nodes = fakenodes, edges = fakeedges) %>%
   concentrate(method = "mocus_rcpp")
topics.seealso: formulate() for creating the function from a boolean equation

topics.name: concentrate
topics.title: concentrate() Function
topics.summary: This function concentrates the boolean equation of a fault tree to find the minimum cutsets in the fault tree.
topics.description: This function concentrates the boolean equation of a fault tree to find the minimum cutsets in the fault tree. It takes a data.frame outputted by the curate() function and applies one of the available MOCUS implementations to perform boolean minimization.

arguments.name: data
arguments.description: (Required) data.frame containing output from curate(). Expects the gates data.frame with columns gate, type, set, and items.

arguments.name: method
arguments.description: (Optional) Character string specifying the minimization algorithm. Default is "mocus_rcpp". Supported values are "mocus_rcpp", "mocus_r", and "mocus_original".

topics.value: A character vector where each element is a minimum cutset represented as a boolean expression (e.g., "A * B" for events A AND B). Each cutset represents a minimal set of events whose simultaneous occurrence causes system failure.
topics.details:
This function performs boolean minimization to identify the minimum cutsets (minimal failure paths) in a fault tree using the MOCUS algorithm:

  • Rcpp MOCUS (method = "mocus_rcpp"):

    • Uses the Rcpp-backed MOCUS implementation (mocus_rcpp())
    • Recommended default for speed on larger trees

  • Pure-R fast MOCUS (method = "mocus_r"):

    • Uses the optimized pure-R implementation (mocus_r())
    • Useful when compiled code is unavailable

  • Original MOCUS (method = "mocus_original"):

    • Uses the original MOCUS implementation (mocus() with method = "mocus_original") to generate all cutsets
    • Returns the cutsets as character strings

Every method then minimises the MOCUS products by absorption: duplicate cutsets and any cutset containing another cutset are dropped. Cutsets are ordered fewest events first, then by the sorted position of their events. Minimum cutsets represent the smallest combinations of basic events that can cause the top event (system failure) to occur.
topics.examples:
# Load dependencies
library(dplyr)
library(tidyfault)

# Load example data into our environment
data("fakenodes")
data("fakeedges")

# Extract minimum cutset from fault tree data
formula <- curate(nodes = fakenodes, edges = fakeedges) %>%
   equate() %>%
   formulate()
curate(nodes = fakenodes, edges = fakeedges) %>%
   concentrate(method = "mocus_rcpp") %>%
   tabulate(formula = formula, method = "mocus_rcpp")
topics.seealso: curate() for preparing gate data for MOCUS method, mocus_rcpp(), mocus_r(), and mocus() for MOCUS implementations, tabulate() for analyzing and summarizing minimum cutsets

topics.name: tabulate
topics.title: tabulate() Function
topics.summary: This function tabulates a data.frame of N minimum cutsets in your fault tree, describing each mincut set, a query used to filter a table of all sets, the number of cutsets that include that mincut, the total number of cutsets leading to failure, and the coverage (percentage of cutsets covered out of total failures) for that mincut.
topics.description: This function tabulates a data.frame of N minimum cutsets in your fault tree, describing each mincut set, a query used to filter a table of all sets, the number of cutsets that include that mincut, the total number of cutsets leading to failure, and the coverage (percentage of cutsets covered out of total failures) for that mincut.
topics.usage:
tabulate(
  data,
  formula,
  method = c("mocus_rcpp", "mocus_r", "mocus_original"),
  query = FALSE
)

arguments.name: data
arguments.description: (Required) Output from concentrate() function. Expects a character vector of minimum cutset expressions (e.g., "A * B").

arguments.name: formula
arguments.description: (Required) Function output from formulate(). Used to generate the truth table for calculating coverage statistics.

arguments.name: method
arguments.description: (Optional) Character string specifying the method used in concentrate(). Default is "mocus_rcpp". Supported values are "mocus_rcpp", "mocus_r", and "mocus_original".

arguments.name: query
arguments.description: (Optional) Logical - Whether to include the query column in the output. Default is FALSE.

topics.value:
A data.frame (tibble) with one row per minimum cutset, containing:

  • mincut: Character string representing the minimum cutset as a boolean expression (e.g., "A * B" for events A AND B)
  • query: Character string containing a filter expression that can be used to identify truth table rows matching this cutset (e.g., "filter(A == 1, B == 1, outcome == 1)") (only included if query = TRUE)
  • cutsets: Integer count of truth table rows (cutsets) that match this minimum cutset and result in system failure
  • failures: Integer count of total truth table rows that result in system failure (same for all rows)
  • coverage: Numeric value (0 to 1) representing the proportion of failure cases covered by this minimum cutset. Calculated as cutsets / failures.
topics.details:
This function analyzes minimum cutsets to quantify their importance in system failure:

  • Truth Table Generation: Uses formula to generate a complete truth table via calculate().
  • Cutset Parsing: Splits each minimum cutset expression into individual events and determines their required states (1 for occurrence, 0 for non-occurrence)
  • Query Construction: Creates filter expressions that identify truth table rows matching each cutset's event combination
  • Coverage Calculation: Counts how many failure cases (rows with outcome == 1) are covered by each minimum cutset, then calculates coverage as a proportion
topics.examples:
# Load dependencies
library(dplyr)
library(tidyfault)

# Load example data into our environment
data("fakenodes")
data("fakeedges")

formula <- curate(nodes = fakenodes, edges = fakeedges) %>%
   equate() %>%
   formulate()
curate(nodes = fakenodes, edges = fakeedges) %>%
   concentrate(method = "mocus_rcpp") %>%
   tabulate(formula = formula, method = "mocus_rcpp")
topics.seealso: concentrate() for generating minimum cutsets, formulate() for creating the function used in truth table generation, calculate() for generating truth tables

topics.name: mocus
topics.title: mocus() Function
topics.summary: This function simplifies a data.frame of gates and their sets identified by curate(), generating each cutset in the fault tree using the MOCUS (Method of Obtaining Cutsets) algorithm.
topics.description: This function simplifies a data.frame of gates and their sets identified by curate(), generating each cutset in the fault tree using the MOCUS (Method of Obtaining Cutsets) algorithm.

arguments.name: data
arguments.description: (Required) data.frame containing gates and their sets, outputted by curate(). Must contain columns gate, type, class, and items (list column of event vectors). The data.frame should have at least one row with class == "top" representing the top event.

arguments.name: method
arguments.description: (Optional) Character string specifying which implementation to run. Default is "mocus_rcpp". Supported values are "mocus_rcpp", "mocus_r", and "mocus_original" (same labels as concentrate() and tabulate()).

topics.value: A list where each element is a character vector representing a cutset (a set of basic events that can cause system failure). Each cutset vector contains the names of basic events. The list includes all cutsets found in the fault tree, not just minimum cutsets. Duplicate events within each cutset are removed (each event appears only once per cutset).
topics.details:
This function implements the MOCUS (Method of Obtaining Cutsets) algorithm, which systematically expands gates in a fault tree to identify all cutsets. The algorithm works as follows:

  • Initialization: Starts with the top event as the first cutset

  • Iterative Expansion: For each cutset containing gate references:

    • Identifies gates that appear in the current cutset
    • For AND gates: Replaces the gate with all its input events (events are combined)
    • For OR gates: Creates separate cutsets for each input path (events are alternatives)
    • Removes the expanded gate from consideration
  • Convergence: Continues until no gates remain in any cutset (only basic events)
  • Deduplication: Removes duplicate events within each cutset

The algorithm handles nested gate structures by repeatedly expanding gates until all references are resolved. AND gates represent events that must all occur together, while OR gates represent alternative failure paths. The result includes all possible cutsets, which can then be minimized using boolean algebra (e.g., via concentrate() with method = "mocus_original"). The default method ("mocus_rcpp") uses the compiled implementation for speed. Use "mocus_r" for a pure-R queue-based variant, or "mocus_original" for the historical R loop used in early versions of the package.
topics.seealso: curate() for preparing the gates data.frame, concentrate() for finding minimum cutsets from the generated cutsets, mocus_rcpp(), mocus_r()

topics.name: mocus_r
topics.title: mocus_r() — Fast Pure-R MOCUS Implementation
topics.summary: Drop-in replacement for mocus() using a queue-based expansion, pre-indexed gate lookup, and integer-encoded events.
topics.description: Drop-in replacement for mocus() using a queue-based expansion, pre-indexed gate lookup, and integer-encoded events. Same inputs/outputs as mocus().

arguments.name: data
arguments.description: data.frame produced by curate(). Must have columns: gate (chr), type (chr/fct), class (chr/fct), items (list of chr vectors).

topics.value: Named list where each element is a character vector of basic events forming one cutset. Identical structure to mocus() output.
topics.details:
Key improvements over original:

  1. Pre-indexes gate table into a named list — zero dplyr::filter() calls inside the loop.
  2. Integer-encodes every event/gate name once up front; all inner-loop operations run on integer vectors (faster %in%, faster unique()).
  3. Queue-based (append-only) expansion — never deletes/reallocates the working list mid-loop. A tail pointer advances; new cutsets are appended to the end.
  4. Expands every gate in a cutset in a single pass rather than one gate per outer-loop iteration.
  5. Convergence is tracked with a simple counter, not by re-flattening the entire list every iteration.

topics.name: mocus_rcpp
topics.title: mocus_rcpp() - Rcpp-Backed MOCUS Implementation
topics.summary: Drop-in replacement for mocus() that delegates the inner expansion loop to compiled C++ via Rcpp.
topics.description: Drop-in replacement for mocus() that delegates the inner expansion loop to compiled C++ via Rcpp. The R layer handles encoding/decoding; C++ handles the queue-based gate expansion with zero R-level allocation in the hot path.

arguments.name: data
arguments.description: data.frame produced by curate(). Must have columns: gate (chr), type (chr/fct), class (chr/fct), items (list of chr vectors).

topics.value: Named list where each element is a character vector of basic events forming one cutset. Identical structure to mocus() / mocus_r() output.
topics.details:
Encoding strategy:

  • Every unique token (gate name or basic event name) is mapped to a positive integer ID once. All C++ operations work on ints.
  • Gate children are stored in a flat integer vector with per-gate start/end offsets, giving cache-friendly sequential access.
  • After C++ returns a list of integer-vector cutsets, R decodes them back to character vectors in one vectorised pass.

topics.name: populate
topics.title: populate() Function
topics.summary: Converts binary outcomes (0/1) to probability outcomes by replacing 1s with event failure probabilities.
topics.description: Converts binary outcomes (0/1) to probability outcomes by replacing 1s with event failure probabilities. The output has the same structure as the input binary outcomes, but with probabilities instead of binary values.

arguments.name: binary_outcomes
arguments.description: (Required) Data frame with binary (0/1) event states. Must have one column per basic event (with event names as column names) and optionally a scenario column. Each row represents one scenario.

arguments.name: event_probs
arguments.description: (Required) Data frame with two columns: event (event names) and probability (failure probabilities in [0, 1]). Must contain probabilities for all events present in binary_outcomes.

topics.value:
A tibble with the same structure as binary_outcomes, where:

  • Values of 1 are replaced with P(event) from event_probs
  • Values of 0 remain as 0

The scenario column (if present) is preserved unchanged.
topics.details: This function transforms binary event states by replacing occurrences (1s) with their corresponding failure probabilities. For each event column, if the binary value is 1 (event occurred), it is replaced with the failure probability P(event) from event_probs. If the binary value is 0 (event did not occur), it remains 0. This creates a data frame suitable for probabilistic evaluation where only occurring events have probability values.
topics.examples:
library(dplyr)
library(tidyfault)

data("db_outcomes_binary")
data("db_probs")

# Convert binary outcomes to probability outcomes
populate(db_outcomes_binary, db_probs)

# Compare: binary has 0/1, probability version has P(event) where binary was 1, 0 otherwise
db_outcomes_binary
populate(db_outcomes_binary, db_probs)
topics.seealso: quantify() for evaluating fault trees with binary or probabilistic inputs, quantify_prob() for computing top event failure probability

topics.name: simulate
topics.title: simulate() Function
topics.summary: This function simulates a fault tree structure with nodes, edges, and basic event probabilities.
topics.description: This function simulates a fault tree structure with nodes, edges, and basic event probabilities. Generates a valid fault tree with one top event, multiple gates (AND/OR), and basic events, ensuring each gate has at least two input events.
topics.usage: simulate(n_gates = 3L, n_basic = 8L, p_range = c(0.01, 0.2), seed = NULL)

arguments.name: n_gates
arguments.description: (Optional) Integer specifying the desired number of internal gates. Default is 3L. The actual number of gates may be reduced if n_basic is insufficient to provide at least two basic events per gate.

arguments.name: n_basic
arguments.description: (Optional) Integer specifying the number of basic events (leaf nodes) in the fault tree. Default is 8L. Must be at least 1.

arguments.name: p_range
arguments.description: (Optional) Numeric vector of length 2 specifying the minimum and maximum probability values for basic events. Default is c(0.01, 0.2). Must satisfy 0 < p_range[1] < p_range[2] < 1.

arguments.name: seed
arguments.description: (Optional) Integer seed for random number generation to ensure reproducibility. Default is NULL (no seed set).

topics.value:
A list with three components:

  • nodes: Data frame with columns id, event, and type. Contains one top event (type "top"), n_gates_eff internal gates (type "and" or "or"), and n_basic basic events (type "not"). The type column is a factor with levels c("top", "and", "or", "not").
  • edges: Data frame with columns from and to, representing connections between nodes. The top event connects to all gates, and gates connect to their assigned basic events.
  • prob: Data frame with columns event and probability, containing probability values for each basic event, sampled uniformly from p_range.
topics.details:
This function generates a valid fault tree structure suitable for use with other tidyfault functions:

  • Gate constraint: Each gate (AND/OR) is guaranteed to have at least two input events. If n_basic < 2 * n_gates, the number of gates is automatically reduced to floor(n_basic / 2).
  • Degenerate case: If n_basic < 2, no internal gates are created; the top event connects directly to all basic events.
  • Gate types: Gate types (AND/OR) are randomly assigned using sample().
  • Event allocation: Basic events are allocated to gates such that each gate receives at least two events, with any remaining events randomly distributed.
  • Event naming: Top event is named "T", gates are named "G1", "G2", etc., and basic events are named "E1", "E2", etc.

The generated fault tree can be used directly with curate(), equate(), formulate(), and other tidyfault workflow functions.
topics.examples:
# Load dependencies
library(tidyfault)

# Simulate a fault tree with default parameters
sim <- simulate(n_gates = 4L, n_basic = 10L, seed = 12345)
sim$nodes
sim$edges
sim$prob

# Use the simulated tree in the tidyfault workflow
gates <- curate(nodes = sim$nodes, edges = sim$edges)
equation <- equate(gates)
formula <- formulate(equation)
cutsets <- concentrate(gates)

# Simulate a larger tree
sim_large <- simulate(n_gates = 10L, n_basic = 25L, 
                     p_range = c(0.05, 0.3), seed = 42)
topics.seealso: curate() for processing the simulated nodes and edges, illustrate() for visualizing the generated fault tree structure

topics.name: quantify
topics.title: quantify() Function
topics.summary: Unified wrapper function for evaluating fault trees.
topics.description: Unified wrapper function for evaluating fault trees. Evaluates whether the top event occurs (binary evaluation) or computes top event failure probability (probabilistic evaluation) based on the prob parameter.
topics.usage: quantify(f, newdata, prob = FALSE, fast = TRUE)

arguments.name: f
arguments.description: (Required) Function from formulate(), with one argument per basic event. Used to identify event names and to evaluate the fault tree.

arguments.name: newdata
arguments.description: (Required) Data for evaluation. When prob = FALSE, this represents binary scenarios (0/1 or TRUE/FALSE) for each basic event. When prob = TRUE, this represents failure probabilities (0 to 1) for each basic event. Can be a tibble/data frame with one column per basic event, a single vector/list, or (for prob = TRUE) a matrix. See details below.

arguments.name: prob
arguments.description: (Optional) Logical. If FALSE (default), performs binary evaluation. If TRUE, computes failure probability.

arguments.name: fast
arguments.description: (Optional) Logical. If TRUE (default), dispatches to optimized implementations (quantify_binary_fast() or quantify_prob_fast()). If FALSE, uses the legacy R implementations (quantify_binary() or quantify_prob()).

topics.value:
A vector of outcomes. The type depends on prob:

  • If prob = FALSE: Returns a logical vector (TRUE = system failure, FALSE = no failure). If newdata is a data frame with multiple rows, returns a vector with one outcome per row. If newdata is a single scenario, returns a single logical value.
  • If prob = TRUE: Returns a numeric vector of top event failure probabilities. If newdata is a single scenario, returns a single numeric value. If newdata has multiple rows, returns a numeric vector with one probability per scenario.

Both modes return vectors in predict()-style format.
topics.details:
This function provides a unified interface for both binary and probabilistic fault tree evaluation:

  • Binary evaluation (prob = FALSE): evaluates whether the top event occurs given binary event states.
  • Probabilistic evaluation (prob = TRUE): computes the top event failure probability from basic event failure probabilities.
  • Fast mode (fast = TRUE): uses optimized paths for larger scenario batches while preserving output semantics.
  • Legacy mode (fast = FALSE): uses the original pure-R implementations.

When prob = FALSE, newdata can be:

  • A data frame with one column per basic event (names from formalArgs(f))
  • A single vector/list (unnamed = positional, or named)
  • Values are logical (TRUE/FALSE) or numeric (0/1)

When prob = TRUE, newdata can be:

  • A single vector or list (one scenario) with probabilities in [0, 1]
  • A data frame or matrix with one row per scenario and columns for each basic event (names must match formalArgs(f))
  • Unnamed vectors are interpreted in formalArgs(f) order
topics.examples:
library(dplyr)
library(tidyfault)
data("fakenodes")
data("fakeedges")

f <- curate(nodes = fakenodes, edges = fakeedges) %>%
  equate() %>%
  formulate()

# Binary evaluation (default): single scenario
f %>% quantify(c(TRUE, TRUE, TRUE, FALSE))
f %>% quantify(c(TRUE, FALSE, TRUE, FALSE))

# Binary evaluation: multiple scenarios
scenarios_tbl <- tibble(
  A = c(1L, 0L, 1L),
  B = c(0L, 1L, 1L),
  C = c(1L, 0L, 0L),
  D = c(0L, 1L, 1L)
)
f %>% quantify(scenarios_tbl)

# Probabilistic evaluation: single scenario
f %>% quantify(c(0.1, 0.2, 0.05, 0.15), prob = TRUE)

# Legacy mode
f %>% quantify(c(0.1, 0.2, 0.05, 0.15), prob = TRUE, fast = FALSE)

# Probabilistic evaluation: multiple scenarios
probs_df <- as.data.frame(replicate(4, runif(100), simplify = FALSE))
names(probs_df) <- formalArgs(f)
f %>% quantify(probs_df, prob = TRUE)
topics.seealso: formulate() for creating the function, calculate() for the full truth table, quantify_binary(), quantify_binary_fast(), quantify_prob(), and quantify_prob_fast()

topics.name: quantify_binary
topics.title: quantify_binary() Function
topics.summary: Evaluates whether the top event occurs (system fails) when given whether each basic event occurs or not.
topics.description: Evaluates whether the top event occurs (system fails) when given whether each basic event occurs or not. Inputs are binary: each event is 0 (did not occur) or 1 (occurred). No probabilities—deterministic evaluation only.

arguments.name: f
arguments.description: (Required) Function from formulate(), with one argument per basic event. Used to identify event names and to evaluate the fault tree.

arguments.name: newdata
arguments.description: (Required) Binary event states (0/1 or TRUE/FALSE) for each basic event. Either a tibble/data frame with one column per basic event (names from formalArgs(f)), or a single vector/list. A single scenario can be an unnamed vector in formalArgs(f) order (e.g. c(TRUE, TRUE, TRUE, FALSE) or c(1, 1, 0, 1)), or a named vector/list. Values are logical (TRUE/FALSE) or numeric (0/1), where 1/TRUE means the event occurred and 0/FALSE means it did not.

topics.value: A logical vector of outcomes (TRUE = system failure, FALSE = no failure). If newdata is a data frame with multiple rows, returns a vector with one outcome per row. If newdata is a single scenario (vector/list), returns a single logical value.
topics.details: No probabilities are used; the function evaluates the fault tree on the given event states. Outcome is TRUE when f(...) >= 1 (system failure). Logical and 0/1 inputs are coerced to 0/1 internally to match calculate() behavior. When newdata is a data frame, evaluation is vectorized: f is called once with vector columns (one element per row), so many scenarios are handled efficiently. Returns only the outcome vector, similar to R's predict() function style.
topics.examples:
library(dplyr)
library(tidyfault)
data("fakenodes")
data("fakeedges")

# Pipe-friendly: single scenario in event order (e.g. A, B, C, D)
curate(nodes = fakenodes, edges = fakeedges) %>%
  equate() %>%
  formulate() %>%
  quantify_binary(c(TRUE, TRUE, TRUE, FALSE))

f <- curate(nodes = fakenodes, edges = fakeedges) %>%
  equate() %>%
  formulate()

# Single scenario: unnamed vector in event order
f %>% quantify_binary(c(TRUE, FALSE, TRUE, FALSE))

# Single scenario: named vector (logical or 0/1)
one_scenario <- setNames(c(TRUE, FALSE, TRUE, FALSE), formalArgs(f))
f %>% quantify_binary(one_scenario)

# Tibble of scenarios: returns vector of outcomes (vectorized, one call to f for all rows)
scenarios_tbl <- tibble(
  A = c(1L, 0L, 1L),
  B = c(0L, 1L, 1L),
  C = c(1L, 0L, 0L),
  D = c(0L, 1L, 1L)
)
f %>% quantify_binary(scenarios_tbl)  # Returns logical vector
topics.seealso: formulate() for creating the function, calculate() for the full truth table, quantify_prob() for top event failure probability given basic event probabilities, quantify() for the unified wrapper function.

topics.name: quantify_prob
topics.title: quantify_prob() Function
topics.summary: Computes the top event failure probability from a fault tree when given basic event failure probabilities.
topics.description: Computes the top event failure probability from a fault tree when given basic event failure probabilities. Assumes independent basic events; uses the full truth table to sum probabilities over all failure combinations.

arguments.name: f
arguments.description: (Required) Function outputted by formulate(), with one argument per basic event. Used to identify event names and, if truth_table is not supplied, to generate the truth table via calculate(f).

arguments.name: newdata
arguments.description: (Required) Failure probabilities (0 to 1) for each basic event. Can be a single vector or list (one scenario), or a data frame or matrix with one row per scenario and columns for each basic event (names must match formalArgs(f)). Unnamed vectors are interpreted in formalArgs(f) order. Values should be in [0, 1], where each value represents the probability that the corresponding basic event occurs.

arguments.name: truth_table
arguments.description: (Optional) Data frame with one column per basic event (0/1) and an outcome column (1 = system failure, 0 = no failure). If provided, the truth table is not recomputed (useful when calculate() was already run).

topics.value: A numeric vector of top-event failure probabilities. If newdata is a single scenario (vector/list or single-row data frame), returns a single numeric value. If newdata has multiple rows (one per scenario), returns a numeric vector with one probability per scenario (same order as rows of newdata). Similar to R's predict() function style.
topics.details: The top event probability is computed exactly via the complete truth table: for each of the 2^n combinations of basic event states, the probability of that combination is the product of newdata[e] for events that occur (1) and 1 - newdata[e] for events that do not (0). The function sums these probabilities over all combinations where outcome == 1. This is exact for independent basic events but has complexity O(2^n); for trees with many basic events, consider using minimal cut set approximations elsewhere. When newdata has multiple rows, the truth table is computed once and all scenarios are evaluated in one pass.
topics.examples:
library(dplyr)
library(tidyfault)
data("fakenodes")
data("fakeedges")

f <- curate(nodes = fakenodes, edges = fakeedges) %>%
  equate() %>%
  formulate()
# Pipe-friendly: probability vector in event order (e.g. A, B, C, D)
curate(nodes = fakenodes, edges = fakeedges) %>%
  equate() %>%
  formulate() %>%
  quantify_prob(c(0.1, 0.2, 0.05, 0.15))

# Named probs (names must match event names in the tree)
probs <- setNames(c(0.1, 0.2, 0.05, 0.15), formalArgs(f))
f %>% quantify_prob(probs)

# Reuse an existing truth table to avoid recomputing
tt <- calculate(f)
f %>% quantify_prob(probs, truth_table = tt)

# Many scenarios at once (vectorized): pass a data frame, one row per scenario
probs_df <- as.data.frame(replicate(4, runif(1000), simplify = FALSE))
names(probs_df) <- formalArgs(f)
f %>% quantify_prob(probs_df, truth_table = tt)  # length-1000 vector
topics.seealso: formulate() for creating the function from a boolean equation, calculate() for generating the truth table, quantify() for evaluating whether the top event occurs given binary (0/1) basic event states. The result matches the FaultTree package when the same tree is built and ftree.calc(DF, use.bdd = TRUE) is used (BDD accounts for repeated basic events; gate-by-gate with use.bdd = FALSE does not).

topics.summary: This function takes nodes and edges from a fault tree, computes a tree layout using tidygraph and ggraph, and returns ggplot-friendly data.frames of nodes, edges, and gate polygons.
topics.description: This function takes nodes and edges from a fault tree, computes a tree layout using tidygraph and ggraph, and returns ggplot-friendly data.frames of nodes, edges, and gate polygons.
topics.usage:
illustrate(
  nodes,
  edges,
  type = c("nodes", "edges", "both", "all"),
  node_key = "id",
  layout = "tree",
  size = 0.25,
  scale_size = FALSE,
  res = 50
)

arguments.name: nodes
arguments.description: (Required) dataset of nodes, including an id field (or whatever is written in node_key)

arguments.name: edges
arguments.description: (Required) dataset of edges, including from and to fields corresponding to the id of each node

arguments.name: type
arguments.description: (Optional) Character string specifying output format. Default is "both", which returns a list with "nodes", "edges", and "gates". Other options: "nodes" returns only node coordinates, "edges" returns only edge coordinates, "all" returns nodes, edges, gates, and pairwise edge data.

arguments.name: node_key
arguments.description: (Optional) Character string naming the column in nodes that contains unique node identifiers. Default is "id".

arguments.name: layout
arguments.description: (Optional) Character string specifying the graph layout algorithm. Default is "tree". "dendrogram" also works well. See ggraph::create_layout() for more layout options (e.g., "fr", "kk", "nicely").

arguments.name: size
arguments.description: (Optional) Numeric value passed to gate() function for constructing polygons. Controls the diameter of gate shapes. Defaults to 0.25. When scale_size = TRUE, this is scaled by the layout extent.

arguments.name: scale_size
arguments.description: (Optional) Logical. If TRUE, scale gate size to the layout extent. Default is FALSE; set to TRUE to try consistent proportions across very different trees.

arguments.name: res
arguments.description: (Optional) Numeric value passed to gate() function for constructing polygons. Controls the number of line segments used to draw curved gate shapes. Defaults to 50.

topics.value:
The return type depends on the type parameter:

  • For type = "nodes": A data.frame with node coordinates (x, y) and all original columns from nodes
  • For type = "edges": A data.frame with edge coordinates formatted for geom_line(), containing columns direction, id, x, y, edge_id

  • For type = "both" (default): A named list of class c("tidyfault_tree", "list") (so plot() dispatches to plot.tidyfault_tree()) with three elements:

    • nodes: Node coordinates data.frame
    • edges: Edge coordinates data.frame
    • gates: Gate polygon coordinates data.frame with x, y columns for drawing gate shapes
  • For type = "all": A named list of class c("tidyfault_tree", "list") with four elements: nodes, edges, gates, and pairwise (edge data with from/to coordinates)
topics.details:
This function prepares fault tree data for visualization with ggplot2 by:

  • Creating a tidygraph object from nodes and edges
  • Computing graph layout coordinates using ggraph::create_layout() with the specified layout algorithm
  • Extracting node coordinates and preserving original node attributes
  • Computing edge coordinates by joining node positions to edge endpoints
  • Generating gate polygon shapes for AND, OR, and top event gates using the gate() function

The output is designed to work seamlessly with ggplot2. Nodes can be plotted with geom_point(), edges with geom_line(), and gates with geom_polygon(). The tree layout algorithm positions nodes hierarchically, making fault tree structure easy to visualize.
topics.seealso: gate() for generating gate polygons, tbl_graph for creating graph objects, create_layout for layout algorithms

topics.name: plot
topics.title: Plot a fault tree from illustrate() output
topics.summary: Plot a fault tree from illustrate() output
topics.description: An S3 method for plot on the tidyfault_tree objects returned by illustrate(type = "both") and illustrate(type = "all"). Calling plot() on any other object dispatches to base R as usual.
topics.usage:
## S3 method for class 'tidyfault_tree'
plot(
  x,
  type_col = "type",
  gate_types = c("and", "or", "top"),
  edge_linewidth = 1,
  gate_linewidth = 0.8,
  gate_alpha = 1,
  point_radius = NULL,
  point_n = 100,
  point_linewidth = 0.8,
  outline_colour = "#0b0405",
  gate_fill = c(top = "#382a54", and = "#395d9c", or = "#3eb4ad", `basic event` =
    "#def5e5"),
  coord_fixed = TRUE,
  theme_void = TRUE,
  expand = 0.2,
  normalize = TRUE,
  basic_radius_ratio = 0.18,
  edge_colour = "#b7c1cb",
  ...
)

arguments.name: x
arguments.description: A tidyfault_tree list returned by illustrate(..., type = "both") or illustrate(..., type = "all"), with elements nodes, edges, and gates.

arguments.name: type_col
arguments.description: Character. Name of the column in x$nodes that holds node type (e.g. "top", "and", "or", "not"). Default is "type".

arguments.name: gate_types
arguments.description: Character vector. Node types that are drawn as gate polygons. Default is c("and", "or", "top").

arguments.name: edge_linewidth
arguments.description: Numeric. Line width for edges. Default 1.

arguments.name: gate_linewidth
arguments.description: Numeric. Outline width for gate polygons. Default 0.8.

arguments.name: gate_alpha
arguments.description: Numeric. Fill opacity for gate polygons (0--1). Default 1.

arguments.name: point_radius
arguments.description: Numeric or NULL. Radius of basic-event circles in data units. If NULL (default), it is estimated from gate sizes (see basic_radius_ratio). Set explicitly (e.g. 0.1) for full control when auto sizing is too small or too big.

arguments.name: point_n
arguments.description: Integer. Number of vertices used to draw each basic-event circle polygon. Default 100.

arguments.name: point_linewidth
arguments.description: Numeric. Outline width for basic-event circles. Default 0.8.

arguments.name: outline_colour
arguments.description: Character. Colour for gate polygon and basic-event outlines. Default "black".

arguments.name: gate_fill
arguments.description: Named character vector of fill colours for gate types (and, or, top) and optionally "basic event" for leaf nodes. Default is c(top = "#382a54", and = "#395d9c", or = "#3eb4ad", "basic event" = "#def5e5"). If NULL, the viridis discrete palette is used instead.

arguments.name: coord_fixed
arguments.description: Logical. If TRUE (default), use equal aspect ratio so shapes are not stretched.

arguments.name: theme_void
arguments.description: Logical. If TRUE (default), remove axes and panel.

arguments.name: expand
arguments.description: Numeric. Fixed padding (in data units) added to the view limits on each side. Default 0.2. For trees with few nodes, the function automatically tightens this to 0.1.

arguments.name: normalize
arguments.description: Logical. If TRUE (default), scale and center node, edge, and gate coordinates so the plot extent is standardized across different trees.

arguments.name: basic_radius_ratio
arguments.description: Numeric. Used only when point_radius = NULL. Basic-event radius is set to this fraction of the median gate extent (each gate's extent is half the sum of its x and y span). Default 0.18. Larger values give bigger circles; smaller values give smaller circles.

arguments.name: edge_colour
arguments.description: Character. Colour for edges. Default "#b7c1cb".
Ignored (for compatibility with the generic plot).

topics.value: A ggplot object.
topics.details: Builds a ggplot of the fault tree using the nodes, edges, and gate polygons returned by illustrate(). Gate nodes (and, or, top) are drawn as polygons with outlines that follow their shape; other nodes (e.g. basic events) are drawn as circle polygons in the same data coordinate system, so their size stays visually consistent relative to the gates. Nodes and gates are labelled using the event column from x$nodes. To avoid pixelated output when saving, use ggsave() with an explicit dpi (e.g. ggsave("plot.png", p, dpi = 300)). Saving from the RStudio Plots pane or at a small size often produces low-resolution images. Basic-event circle size when point_radius = NULL: the function takes each gate polygon's extent (half of x-span + y-span), then uses the median of those extents times basic_radius_ratio. So circle size follows a typical gate size. It can still look too small or too big when gate sizes vary a lot (e.g. one large top gate and many small gates), or when the layout is very compact or very spread out. In those cases, set point_radius explicitly (e.g. 0.08 or 0.15) or adjust basic_radius_ratio.
topics.examples:
data(it_security_nodes, it_security_edges, package = "tidyfault")
ill <- illustrate(nodes = it_security_nodes, edges = it_security_edges, type = "both")
p <- plot(ill)
## Not run:
ggsave("fault_tree.png", p, dpi = 300)
## End(Not run)

topics.name: gate
topics.title: gate() Function
topics.summary: This internal function gathers all gate polygons for a set of supplied gate types and their x and y coordinates.
topics.description: This internal function gathers all gate polygons for a set of supplied gate types and their x and y coordinates.

arguments.name: data
arguments.description: (Required) data.frame of nodes with coordinates. Must include columns for x and y coordinates, and at least one row where the gate type is "and", "or", or "top".

arguments.name: group
arguments.description: (Default = "id") Character string naming the column in data that contains unique identifiers for grouping nodes. Default is "id".

arguments.name: gate
arguments.description: (Default = "type") Character string naming the column in data that contains gate types. Must contain values "and", "or", or "top". Default is "type".

arguments.name: size
arguments.description: (Default = 1) Numeric value controlling the diameter of gate polygons. Larger values create bigger gate shapes.

arguments.name: res
arguments.description: (Default = 50) Numeric value controlling the number of line segments used to draw curved gate shapes. Higher values create smoother curves but require more computation.

topics.value: A data.frame (tibble) with columns x and y containing coordinate pairs that define gate polygon shapes. The data.frame is grouped by the group and gate columns, with one polygon per unique combination. Coordinates are centered at the node's position and scaled according to size.
topics.details:
This function generates polygon coordinates for visualizing gates in fault tree diagrams:

  • Filters nodes to only those with gate types ("and", "or", "top")
  • Groups nodes by their identifier and gate type
  • Calls get_gate() for each group to generate the appropriate polygon shape
  • Returns all polygon coordinates in a single data.frame suitable for use with geom_polygon() in ggplot2

The function is typically called internally by illustrate() but can be used directly to generate gate shapes for custom visualizations. Each gate type (AND, OR, top event) has a distinct shape generated by the corresponding gate_*() function.
topics.seealso: get_gate() for generating individual gate polygons, gate_and() for AND gate shapes, gate_or() for OR gate shapes, gate_top() for top event shapes

topics.name: gate_and
topics.title: gate_and() Function
topics.summary: This function produces the AND gate polygons for fault trees.
topics.description: This function produces the AND gate polygons for fault trees.

arguments.name: size
arguments.description: (Default = 2) Numeric value controlling the base size/diameter of the AND gate shape. The shape is scaled proportionally. Default is 2.

arguments.name: res
arguments.description: (Required) Numeric value describing the resolution, or number of line segments used to draw the curved portions of the gate shape. Higher values create smoother curves. Typically set to 50 or higher.

topics.value: A data.frame (tibble) with columns x and y containing coordinate pairs that define an AND gate polygon shape. The coordinates are centered at the origin (0, 0) and represent a rounded rectangle shape characteristic of AND gates in fault tree diagrams. The shape is symmetric and can be translated and scaled as needed.
topics.details:
This function generates the geometric shape for AND gates in fault tree visualizations:

  • Creates a rounded rectangle shape with curved sides
  • Uses square root functions to generate smooth curves on the left and right sides
  • Centers the shape at the origin (0, 0) for easy translation
  • The shape follows standard fault tree analysis conventions where AND gates are represented as rounded rectangles

The AND gate shape is generated using mathematical curves: the left side uses sqrt(x) and the right side uses sqrt(size - x) to create symmetric rounded edges. The shape is then centered vertically and horizontally.

topics.name: gate_or
topics.title: gate_or() Function
topics.summary: This function produces the OR gate polygons for fault trees.
topics.description: This function produces the OR gate polygons for fault trees.

arguments.name: size
arguments.description: (Default = 2) Numeric value controlling the base size/diameter of the OR gate shape. The shape is scaled proportionally. Default is 2.

arguments.name: res
arguments.description: (Required) Numeric value describing the resolution, or number of line segments used to draw the curved portions of the gate shape. Higher values create smoother curves. Typically set to 50 or higher.

topics.value: A data.frame (tibble) with columns x and y containing coordinate pairs that define an OR gate polygon shape. The coordinates are centered at the origin (0, 0) and represent a curved shape with a concave top and convex bottom, characteristic of OR gates in fault tree diagrams. The shape is symmetric and can be translated and scaled as needed.
topics.details:
This function generates the geometric shape for OR gates in fault tree visualizations:

  • Creates a curved shape with a concave top edge and convex bottom edge
  • Uses square root functions with different scaling factors for the top and bottom curves
  • Combines two curve segments (top and bottom) to form the complete gate shape
  • Centers the shape at the origin (0, 0) for easy translation
  • The shape follows standard fault tree analysis conventions where OR gates are represented as curved shapes

The OR gate shape uses different mathematical curves for the top (concave, using 1/size * sqrt(x)) and bottom (convex, using size * sqrt(x)) to create the distinctive curved appearance. The two curve segments are combined and centered to form the final polygon.

topics.name: gate_top
topics.title: gate_top() Function
topics.summary: This function produces the top event gate polygons for fault trees.
topics.description: This function produces the top event gate polygons for fault trees.

arguments.name: size
arguments.description: (Default = 2) Numeric value controlling the size of the top event rectangle. The shape is a square with sides of length size. Default is 2.

arguments.name: res
arguments.description: (Required) Numeric value describing the resolution. For rectangular shapes, this parameter is accepted for consistency with other gate functions but does not affect the output (rectangles don't require curve resolution).

topics.value: A data.frame (tibble) with columns x and y containing coordinate pairs that define a rectangular top event polygon shape. The coordinates are centered at the origin (0, 0) and represent a square shape characteristic of top events in fault tree diagrams. The shape can be translated and scaled as needed.
topics.details:
This function generates the geometric shape for top events in fault tree visualizations:

  • Creates a simple rectangular (square) shape
  • Defines the rectangle using corner coordinates
  • Centers the shape at the origin (0, 0) for easy translation
  • The shape follows standard fault tree analysis conventions where top events are represented as rectangles

The top event shape is the simplest gate shape, consisting of a square defined by four corner points. The rectangle is created by specifying the four corners in order, then centering the shape by offsetting coordinates by size/2 in both x and y directions. Unlike AND and OR gates, the top event shape does not use curved edges, so the res parameter is included for consistency but doesn't affect the output.

topics.name: get_gate
topics.title: get_gate() Function
topics.summary: This function produces the gate polygons for a set of supplied gate types and their x and y coordinates.
topics.description: This function produces the gate polygons for a set of supplied gate types and their x and y coordinates.

arguments.name: x
arguments.description: (Required) Numeric value or vector representing the x coordinate(s) of the gate center in the layout.

arguments.name: y
arguments.description: (Required) Numeric value or vector representing the y coordinate(s) of the gate center in the layout.

arguments.name: gate
arguments.description: (Required) Character vector of gate type names. Must contain one or more of "top", "and", or "or". If multiple values are provided, only the first unique value is used.

arguments.name: size
arguments.description: (Default = 1) Numeric value controlling the diameter of the gate polygon. The shape is scaled proportionally around the center point. Default is 1.

arguments.name: res
arguments.description: (Default = 50) Numeric value controlling the resolution (number of line segments) used to draw curved gate shapes. Higher values create smoother curves. Default is 50.

topics.value: A data.frame (tibble) with columns x and y containing coordinate pairs that define the gate polygon shape. The coordinates are centered at the provided (x, y) position and scaled according to size. The shape depends on the gate type: AND gates have a rounded rectangle shape, OR gates have a curved shape, and top events have a rectangular shape.
topics.details:
This function is a wrapper that selects and generates the appropriate gate shape based on the gate type:

  • Determines the gate type from the gate parameter (uses first unique value if multiple provided)
  • Calls the appropriate shape-generating function: gate_and() for AND gates, gate_or() for OR gates, or gate_top() for top events
  • Scales and translates the base shape to match the specified (x, y) coordinates and size parameter
  • Returns coordinates ready for use with geom_polygon() in ggplot2

The function handles coordinate transformation using scales::rescale() to position the gate shape correctly. Each gate type has a distinct visual representation following standard fault tree analysis conventions.
topics.seealso: gate_and() for AND gate shape generation, gate_or() for OR gate shape generation, gate_top() for top event shape generation
